Paragraph: Summary of Passage: Performing one's own designated duty—even if imperfectly executed—is far superior to performing another person's duty exceptionally well. Experiencing setbacks in one's natural path is preferable, whereas attempting to adopt another's role breeds fear and psychological instability.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna's temptation to abandon his duty as a warrior and adopt the quiet life of an ascetic to avoid uncomfortable conflict.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna asserts that following one's own natural path (sva-dharma) is far better than adopting another's path (para-dharma), even if another's path seems easier or cleaner. Copying others creates fear (bhayavaha).
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna is grounded in the necessity of fulfilling his own authentic role in life.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Authentic Living: Honoring your true calling and capability instead of imitating others
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Avoiding Imposter Syndrome: Refraining from stepping into roles for which you are unsuited
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Alignment with Core Aptitude: Directing your energy toward duties that match your genuine nature

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Sreyan sva-dharmo vigunah (One's own duty, even if flawed, is superior)
Para-dharmo bhayavahah (Following another's path brings danger and fear)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: It is far better to perform one's own prescribed duty (sva-dharma), even if flawed, than to take up another's duty (para-dharma). Sticking to one's natural duty brings inner harmony, whereas imitating others leads to spiritual danger.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Trying to live someone else's life or career out of social expectation leads to anxiety and imposter syndrome. Embracing your authentic skills and responsibilities—flaws included—fosters real self-esteem and resilience.
